context: The input is choices = [4, 4, 5] at indices 0, 1, and 2. “First 4” and “second 4” distinguish indices 0 and 1. The figure marks the second 4 with a hat. Both have numerical value 4. The array is sorted, target = 9, and each circle shows the remaining target.
description: Each index may be used at most once, and subset order does not matter. After choosing index i, begin the next round at start = i + 1. This skips earlier indices (rule 2) and prevents reuse of the current index (rule 3).

At the root, the second 4 has i = 1 greater than start = 0 and equals the preceding candidate. Rule 4 skips this same-round duplicate. After prefix [first 4], a new call starts at start = 1. The second 4 now has i = 1 equal to start, so i > start is false and it can be chosen. Choosing it leaves 1. Only 5 remains ahead, exceeding 1 and triggering a break under rule 1.

The first table explains the four scissors symbols. The next table lists each prefix and candidate. No pruned branch generates a recursive call. Rules 2 and 3 skip indices directly through start = i + 1, so the loop never tries those candidates. The figure includes them for comparison. Choosing the first 4 after [first 4, second 4] is marked as returning to an earlier index (rule 2). Its index, 0, is also already on the path.

frames.explanation: Only one path reaches zero: choose the first 4, then 5, giving [4, 5].
frames.title: Four pruning rules for subset sum II

summary: Search the sorted array [4, 4, 5] for subsets that sum to 9. Four pruning rules leave the unique solution [4, 5].

tables.caption: Meaning of the four pruning rules
rows: The choice would take the sum above 9, making the remaining target negative
Returning to an earlier index repeats a combination in a different order
Reusing the array index just chosen
Trying an equal-valued candidate again in the same round
